content:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

title: A Little The Crucible. A Little The Craft. A Lot of Catholic Guilt.
summary: The Body opens with a fake-out. The new Netflix show’s title card bears its name in a Gothic typeface—fittingly monastic for a series set in a Catholic high school. But upon closer look, the imposing script is specifically referencing a more modern aesthetic: the rhinestone-studded Juicy Couture log...
content:
The Body opens with a fake-out. The new Netflix show’s title card bears its name in a Gothic typeface—fittingly monastic for a series set in a Catholic high school. But upon closer look, the imposing script is specifically referencing a more modern aesthetic: the rhinestone-studded Juicy Couture logo, frequently seen in the early aughts emblazoned across the backsides of velour tracksuits. That choice, however, is startlingly apropos: The Body, set in 2004, is as much concerned with girlhood—and all of its material obsessions and hormonal impulses—as it is with the religious experience. Here, in fact, these often seem to be considered one and the same.

The show, a mix of campy horror and psychodrama, has topped the streaming charts; it has also earned the ire of some viewers who consider its premise blasphemous—the story of a Catholic school’s girls’ dance team called the Lions, whose members reckon with their beliefs in the fallout of a traumatic event: In the series premiere, the teens lead an Ecstasy-powered, mock-satanic hazing ritual at a Halloween party, after which one new member, Grace (played by Sofia Wylie), has several seizures. She then dies but somehow comes back to life—what one girl drolly describes as a Jesus-like resurrection.

As Grace lies comatose, her teammates question whether her condition is the result of Satan preying on them for invoking his name during the initiation, and whether the “visions” they each start having are the result of mass hysteria; the series makes a valid case for both possibilities. The Body revels in the teens’ more garden-variety exploits as well, in explicit scenes (back-seat sex, raunchy drawings) that are par for the course with today’s teen dramas. The difference here, however, is that this show often depicts messing with drugs and messing with the devil as equally dangerous adolescent acts of rebellion.

[Read: The Americans having the most sex]

Most of the Lions initially treat Catholicism as a joke, and they want everyone else to see them laughing. One girl sports a tight-fitting T-shirt that reads Jesus saves. I spend. Before the Halloween party, the co-captain Elise (Sara Boustany) warns the other dancers that donning provocative schoolgirl costumes is “redundant.” The event itself is held at what the St. Mark’s students call the “Devil’s House,” an abandoned convent whose former inhabitants are rumored to have lost their minds. The night offers the teens a chance to flip a symbolic middle finger to a religious institution that demands their subservience. Defiance is a form of self-control, and they exercise it in the most extreme ways possible.

But after Grace seemingly begins to haunt her teammates, the girls’ faith takes on a visceral—even punishing—quality. Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), the outsider classmate who once spoke in tongues before forcing her way on to the dance team, encourages the teens’ mounting fears of divine persecution. In response, they each begin confessing their sins, religious and social. (“I made out with Katie’s dad!” one of them admits. Another shouts that she’s “part of the fucking chess club!”) What’s really pouring out in these girls’ revelations, however, is all of the pent-up steam that can accumulate for a teen stuck in a Catholic-school hothouse.

The girls have long been fed a diet of mixed messages when it comes to their physical and emotional selves. Their teachers tell them that their bodies are temples they should keep pure. Pop culture, meanwhile, tells them that their bodies are tools of pleasure. They’ve been raised in the era of postfeminist girl power—the Spice Girls likely soundtracked their elementary-school years—and absorbed the notion that their destiny is theirs to control. But their faith, in the show’s rendering, still shoves women toward the back.

It’s no wonder that when the Lions begin to suspect that they can directly affect their own lives, they crack. Their identities, the show seems to argue, are inextricable from the rules, rituals, and cultural influences that dominate their lives. The Body, then, works as a study in what happens when young women break from the strictures that keep them in line. These characters feel as ecstatic as saints and as tortured as martyrs, sometimes in the same hour—being a teenage girl has room for all expressions of faith.

title: This Thanksgiving, I’m Grateful for Claude
summary: It used to be that on a typical afternoon, my husband would send me a message asking whether he needed to grab anything for dinner on his way home from work. Ah, dinner. “What do we eat?” I would say. “Well, there’s always fajitas,” he’d suggest. “Or I guess we could do tortellini again,” I’d offer....
content:
It used to be that on a typical afternoon, my husband would send me a message asking whether he needed to grab anything for dinner on his way home from work. Ah, dinner. “What do we eat?” I would say. “Well, there’s always fajitas,” he’d suggest. “Or I guess we could do tortellini again,” I’d offer. Or maybe one of us would say, half-heartedly, that we should try something new. (Cue some Googling for easy family-dinner recipes.)

On our best days, this conversation would occur midday, leaving time for a fridge check. More often, it would occur at 5:15 p.m. while I was standing on the sidelines of my kids’ swimming lesson or supervising a playground trip, straining to remember whether we already had mozzarella. Hours later, and about 13 minutes before bedtime was theoretically supposed to begin, we’d all sit down to a hastily prepared meal.

Repeated over years, this quotidian ritual started to become agonizing—so much so that I empathized deeply with the author of an essay published last year in The New York Times, headlined “Why I Had to Kill Family Dinner.” My own mom and dad—the parents of five children—eventually did just that, slipping into a “fend for yourselves” system on most nights by the time I was a preteen. My husband and I, though, were desperate to avoid such an outcome.

For one thing, I really enjoy cooking, as does he; it’s not a task we want to abandon entirely. Contingent on having all of the requisite ingredients in front of us, we like messing around and trying new recipes too. The trouble is, we struggle to reliably ensure that the ingredients are, in fact, in front of us. It’s the planning—the “mental load,” as they say—that isn’t happening.

For another, my husband and I want to be the sort of couple who can regularly host people for dinner, a pastime that’s been receding from American life. The share of people in the United States who’ve given or attended a dinner party at least once in the past year fell from 70 percent to 57 percent over the past three decades; just 12 percent of Americans host friends or family monthly, down a whopping 70 percent since 1975. Yet despite our best intentions, my husband and I rarely have our stuff together enough to host. This means that we tend to mooch our way through shared festivities, readily showing up wherever we’re invited but finding it a struggle to reciprocate on our own turf.

So when I started seeing posts online from parents describing the ways that AI is revolutionizing their meal planning, I was intrigued. Like many people, I have grave concerns about artificial intelligence and what it means for the future of humanity. I worry that even if AI doesn’t lead to our extinction, it will further erode the human element from our lives and drive us deeper into isolation. But when it comes to dinner, I realized, AI might have the potential to move the needle in the other direction—to ease the logistical burden of meal planning and, in doing so, help people find their way back to one another.

I’ve spent a lot of time reflecting on why my husband and I find such a simple task—choosing what to feed people—so difficult. And I’ve landed on a few reasons: First, before you can pick what’s for dinner, you’ve got to be able to remember what your options are. We’ve never developed a good system for this. I can’t tell you the number of times we’ve tried a recipe, loved it, and said “We need to add that into the rotation” only for that recipe to be almost immediately forgotten in the graveyard of bookmarked recipes spread across our digital devices.

Beyond that, our mutual lack of strong preferences can be a real disadvantage. We learned this lesson the hard way while planning our wedding. I assumed, naively, that being the sort of person who didn’t care whether we ate chicken or salmon would be an asset. Wrong. The ability to shrug one’s shoulders at any given outcome is helpful only when you are not the one making a decision. This of course applies to family dinner: You have to make a choice, not only for yourself but also on behalf of everyone in attendance.

AI doesn’t share these deficiencies. Its capacity for recalling every protein-rich meal our kids enjoy that might be suitable for a cold week in November is limitless. It is also immune to decision paralysis. So, several weeks ago, I decided to see whether it could simply take over the task of meal planning entirely. We use Claude, and I fed it a document listing several recipes that my family likes or that I had a hunch we’d like, along with our lunch and breakfast staples. I told it that we’re a family of five and appreciate having leftovers. Then I asked it to pick five dinners and make a grocery list.

Week 1 went exactly to plan. It sounds sort of silly, but: We made dinner easily every night and ate it together. Because we were choosing from a short list of meals for which we already had the ingredients, we didn’t agonize over what to cook. And because two of those meals resulted in leftovers, we entered the weekend with everything ready for dinner Saturday night, which I’m pretty sure is a family first—one with unanticipated prosocial consequences. We were already planning to meet my sister and her family at a festival around the corner from our home that day. And in the fridge and pantry, we had all that we needed for a Tuscan chicken pasta. After the fest, we invited everyone to our house. We cooked. We ate. Our guests left smiling and satisfied.

Week 2 was a true test of our new system: My husband was out of town, which left me alone with the three kids. I confided this to Claude, and it suggested some quick, simple recipes. I wouldn’t say that things went smoothly. After one chaotic afternoon—school event, ballet class—I came close to abandoning the meal plan entirely. I threw everything into the oven and hurried to get the baby to bed. When I emerged later, my daughter wondered aloud, “Is the chicken in the oven?” The chicken! I opened the oven to find the thighs a bit charred on top and weighed whether takeout wasn’t such a bad idea. But then my daughter, gazing over my shoulder at the scorched meat, piped up again: “It’s nice to sit down to a nice, healthy meal.” And it was.

By Week 3, I could feel myself getting a little ambitious. Theoretically, there was no end to the number of Murray-suited meals Claude could keep at the ready. I searched through old chats and bookmarks for loved but forgotten recipes to add to our document, which I renamed “The Rotation.” Forty recipes and counting.

This was also the week of Halloween, and my sister was hosting her annual party, where dressing in costume and bringing a dish to share are strongly encouraged. For a fleeting moment, I considered finding an excuse not to attend. But I sallied bravely forth, ordering a pair of rabbit ears from Amazon and asking Claude to include a dish suitable for a potluck in our meal plan. It picked chili. I started second-guessing its decision: I’ve never made chili. Isn’t chili a little predictable? What if my chili has to compete with other, better chilis? But I stuffed down these concerns. Claude had spoken. Chili it was. And the dish got nothing but compliments—including the approval of my 1-year-old, who couldn’t get enough of it.

We are now several weeks into this experiment. And yes, we’ve had some hiccups along the way. At one point, Claude got confused, and instead of picking from our approved recipe list, it suggested that I make something called “Mummy Hot Dogs,” which are “hot dogs wrapped in crescent dough strips with candy eyes.” (No thanks.) This was fixed with clearer instructions never to depart from “The Rotation,” which continues to expand every week.

Now I can feel my borrowed confidence expanding, just in time for the holidays. We announced to our families that we’d like to host everyone for a night of caroling—including dinner—in mid-December. We haven’t quite worked out the menu yet. But we have a hack for that.

title: Measles, MAHA, and the Future of Disease in America
summary:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket CastsUpdated at 9:35 a.m. ET on November 26, 2026

The measles are back. The U.S. achieved measles-elimination status back in 2000 and then lost it earlier this month. To date, there have been more than 40 outbreaks and 5,800 cas...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Updated at 9:35 a.m. ET on November 26, 2026

The measles are back. The U.S. achieved measles-elimination status back in 2000 and then lost it earlier this month. To date, there have been more than 40 outbreaks and 5,800 cases since the year began, according to the CDC data—a significant jump from the 2,289 confirmed cases last year. Such an outbreak is exactly the sort of thing lawmakers who questioned Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s anti-vaccine activism during his confirmation hearings had been worried about. “Frankly, you frighten people,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said at the time, before urging Kennedy to promise “never to say vaccines aren’t medically safe when they in fact are.”

Since the measles-elimination status was removed, Kennedy has argued that Americans need to work to rebuild trust in vaccines. As the Make America Healthy Again movement comes face-to-face with the dangers of abjuring scientific consensus, my colleague Tom Bartlett joins me to discuss an outstanding question: Where do we go from here?

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Tom Bartlett: Most people in this country are in favor of vaccination—Democrats, Republicans. We’re actually not that polarized on that issue. What we have is a very vocal group of people, including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have been pushing this contrarian and erroneous message about the dangers of vaccines for a long time. But if you get to the point where you have parents sort of forgoing normal childhood immunization, yeah, we should be worried.

[Music]

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to talk about measles and MAHA. During his confirmation hearing to become the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services in 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said:

Robert F. Kennedy Jr.: I wanna thank President Trump for entrusting me to deliver on his promise to make America healthy again.

Harris: But last week, after nearly three decades, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States has lost its measles-elimination status. Measles was eliminated back in 2000 because people were getting their shots, but in recent years, vaccination rates have fallen as misinformation about their safety has proliferated.

When the elimination status was removed, Kennedy Jr. said, quote, “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust.” But many scientists and doctors argue Kennedy, a noted vaccine skeptic, is a large part of the reason why that trust was broken in the first place.

What does it mean that measles are back? And where does the movement to make America healthy again go from here? My colleague Tom Bartlett joins me to discuss. Let’s get to questions.

Tom, thank you so much for joining me.

Bartlett: Thanks, Adam.

Harris: I wanna start with a basic question. How did we get here? What does it mean that the U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status?

Bartlett: In technical terms, it means that we’ve had at least 12 months where a single strain has been transmitted throughout the country. And so you have this essentially unbroken stretch where people have been getting the measles. So that’s sort of the technical definition. But I mean, I think measles is now—it was ruled eliminated in 2000, which means there were still sporadic outbreaks, but it was basically under control.

And so losing that elimination status is really a sign that it’s really no longer in control, and that there’s this work to be done. In terms of how we got here, I think the key thing that people point to is pandemic disruption in vaccination schedules and areas where that vaccination rate among kindergartners fell below 95 percent, which is the herd-immunity threshold. So that’s kind of the basics of why we’re here.

Harris: I guess how big of a deal is it that we’ve lost the status? If it’s sort of moving from sporadic to a sort of continuous strain of infections, is this, like, COVID-size, or what’s the scale that we’re thinking of here?

Bartlett: So right now, these infections have been mostly confined to severely undervaccinated communities. So it’s a lot of Mennonite communities and Amish communities. And for the most part, that’s where it stayed. And so, are we looking at COVID-wide outbreaks? I think the short answer is no, but we also just don’t know where this ends, how much bigger this gets. We do have undervaccinated areas of the country that aren’t predominantly Mennonite or Amish. They haven’t, for the most part, been affected significantly. But I think we don’t know where this ends.

And then just in general, it’s a sign that something needs to be done, a vaccination push or something, because it’s no longer eliminated. We thought we were moving toward eradication, which would be: We don’t have any outbreaks at all, even sporadic ones. And this is really a big step back.

So it’s really a sign that we’ve taken a step back, and that’s not what we would hope to do from a public-health point of view.

Harris: I think most people don’t necessarily have a context for measles at this point, or if they do, it’s so far removed, and we can talk about it in terms of the numbers, but there is a real sort of human impact to this. These are families who are experiencing the loss of loved ones.

You’ve done a lot of reporting in these communities. You’ve talked to some of these families. Can you sort of humanize this a little bit for folks? What are these families going through?

Bartlett: Yeah, you’re right. It’s not something that most of us sort of under a certain age have any experience. It’s also not something that most doctors have encountered, which has been an issue too, because how do they recognize cases? It’s not something they’re used to seeing normally. But yeah, for those families, I’ve talked to families—Amish families and Mennonite families—you know, sort of the obvious: It’s frightening. They’ll have children; often these families are quite large, and so all the children will be sick at the same time. Measles is among the most communicable diseases that we have. It spreads very easily and very quickly, and so an entire family or entire community can become infected. And so, yeah, frightening when you have several children who are ill.

I’ve certainly talked to families who had a couple of kids who were extremely ill, trouble breathing, you know, dehydrated. It affects people differently, and in some cases it is fairly mild. In other cases, it’s really severe, and it’s sort of hard to know exactly how it’s gonna happen. But certainly, these are families that are dealing with tremendous grief. Losing a child is, you know, I think no greater grief. And I think a lot of them are—they were caught off-guard by this. I mean, they didn’t see this coming. It hadn’t been a problem in their communities, really, either for a long time.

Harris: Speaking of they didn’t see this coming, there was one family you spoke to who didn’t even know that their child had become a sort of national headline after their death. I imagine, you were able to get more information from the person who was doing the autopsy than the parents were, it seemed. How did they sort of navigate that sort of information gap?

Bartlett: When I spoke to them—this is a family in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, which is really one of the counties that’s been hardest hit. It has a large Amish community. That disease has really gone throughout that community, and really everyone that family knew, or seemingly everyone they knew, had been affected. When I spoke to them in August, they were certainly frustrated that they had been getting so little information from the state, and what became a national controversy about the death of their child that they were pretty much entirely unaware of. And they didn’t realize it had become this source of controversy between the health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the governor of Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro. It was certainly my impression that they weren’t getting sort of clear communication about what was going on and what the results of the autopsy were on their child.

Harris: One of the things that we’ve kind of seen surfacing is this idea of comorbidities, right? It was similar with COVID, where it’s like, Oh, they didn’t die of COVID. They died of excess fluid in their lungs, or, They died from pneumonia that was exacerbated here. Similarly with measles, right? It opens children up to greater susceptibilities to different viruses. And so where someone might say, It was measles, and the other person might say, It was the spleen, or someone might say, It was measles, someone else might say, It was pneumonia.

How is that conversation, the comorbidities piece of this, affecting the measles dialogue at the moment?

Bartlett: I think that’s been one of the most interesting things in terms of how people are taking this. So there’s a certain group of people who wanna say, Well, if you have these comorbidities, or if you’re vulnerable, you’re immunocompromised, and you die from the measles, that, quote-unquote, “didn’t count.”

But this is the reason we sort of do universal vaccination, because we have people who are going to be more vulnerable to diseases, and we want to keep them from getting it. So I mean, that part of the debate, I think, has been sort of misleading and frustrating.

And it’s not just children. So one of the deaths in Pennsylvania was a mother, and she did have a number of comorbidities. And no doubt, that factored into her death. But when I was speaking to the coroner there, he said this was a mother who was regularly making dinner for her children, was living a normal life, and was dealing with the issues that she had, and she was unvaccinated for measles. She got the measles and she died. Comorbidities don’t make those deaths any less of a tragedy, nor do they undermine the case for universal vaccination. To my mind, they strengthen the case for universal vaccination.

Harris: I wanna talk about RFK Jr. a bit here and his role. He said that measles was beginning to spread in the U.S. before his term as secretary, but the spread has gotten worse since then. So what has his response been to the outbreak and also to the elimination status?

Bartlett: I think his response has been confusing, honestly. I mean, he has said, a range of things that are contradictory. A good thing to note in the background that’s just simply true is that he is a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

When you look at things that he said before becoming health secretary, where he has said, It’s basically misinformation that measles is deadly, or he said that we don’t have proof that the vaccine is safe or effective, which we do. So I mean, that’s the background. But he’s also sort of touted things, touted vitamin A, which can be a treatment in some cases but is in no way a substitute for vaccination.

You know, a very mixed message and sort of not what public-health officials would certainly hope that someone in his position would say.

Harris: And I guess with the strength of the anti-vax movement in the U.S., are there other diseases on the horizon that folks should be worried about? If it’s not just the sort of skepticism about measles but also the skepticism about these other vaccines?

Bartlett: Yeah, it’s a totally reasonable question. I’ve spent a lot of time talking to people who are very much in that anti-vaccine world and who would say they don’t want their children vaccinated for any disease, including, say, polio. That’s still a relatively small part of the population. A thing generally to note is most people in this country are in favor of vaccination—Democrats, Republicans. We’re actually not that polarized on that issue. What we have is a very vocal group of people, including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have been pushing this contrarian and erroneous message about the dangers of vaccines for a long time. But I think that’s a thing to be concerned about if you get to the point where you have parents sort of forgoing normal childhood immunization, yeah. Should be worried.

[Music]

Harris: When we come back, we’re going to talk about that very vocal group of people and where they go from here.

[Break]

Harris: So we’ve been talking about disease and vaccine skepticism, sort of a tenet of the MAHA movement, which some argue helped propel Trump back into the White House in 2024. But MAHA is also associated with nutrition, exercise, wanting to reform food and agricultural systems. So two years after the 2024 election, where does the MAHA movement stand, and what’s its sort of relationship to the president at the moment?

Bartlett: If you listen to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and some of his close supporters, they will talk about its successes. They haven’t achieved many of the things that they hoped to achieve, and they’ve also had a number of setbacks over sort of key issues.

And so, one thing to say sort of politically is: MAHA had been touted as potentially an enormous influence on the midterms, and they really weren’t. Two of the candidates they really pushed were Zach Lahn in Iowa and Ken Paxton in Texas. Both of those candidates lost.

The race that they really spent a lot of money on as a primary race was against Bill Cassidy, who’s a Republican. And so MAHA hasn’t been this force for Republicans politically that it was sort of touted as.

In terms of what its achievements have been, they will say they’ve raised issues that are important to the American public. But in terms of solid accomplishments, they will point to things like the limits on SNAP purchases for soda, which is sort of state-by-state, or they will point to a change in dietary guidelines. But there haven’t been, sort of, the solid wins for MAHA that they had hoped.

Harris: What were their reasons for backing these specific candidates? For backing Paxton or for sort of running against Cassidy? Were there sort of ideological goals that they were after there?

Bartlett: Paxton has been willing to sort of make announcements about going after sort of industries that MAHA is against, so sort of questioning vaccines or the food industry or things like that. Cassidy was really targeted seemingly because he, even though he voted to confirm Kennedy, had pushed back in a number of instances on things that Kennedy wanted to do and questioned him on vaccines. Cassidy’s a physician, has expertise in this area. And so I think that was the reason there.

Harris: Are there priorities that MAHA has had to sort of leave on the table? I know one of the big things was sort of getting the big money out of medicine, out of health care. But it seems that’s one of those priorities that they’ve sort of shelved a little bit. So are there other priorities that they’ve sort of left on the table?

Bartlett: Their biggest defeat, I would say, this year, at least in terms of what MAHA activists wanted, was around the herbicide glyphosate. And they really wanted action limiting glyphosate. In fact, Trump back in February issued an executive order really, under the Defense Production Act, sort of protecting the supply of glyphosate. That was a huge—

Harris: Sorry. When you say “glyphosate,” can you just explain that to those of us who aren’t scientists?

Bartlett: Yeah, of course. So glyphosate is a really commonly used weed killer, and so there are concerns about whether that’s linked to cancer or not. There’s some dispute about how strong those links are. And so that’s been a long-standing goal of Kennedy’s, even before he became health secretary, to sort of oppose glyphosate, and that had been one of the things that activists had hoped he would do. And so that hasn’t happened. So that’s one thing that’s been left on the table.

Really, there’s a whole slew of issues that MAHA has talked about that really haven’t come to fruition.

Harris: We’ve seen a sort of fracturing of the MAHA movement based on the fact that they aren’t able to get some of those priorities that they were hoping for, the sort of return on investments. Is that fracturing of the MAHA movement real?

Bartlett: Yeah, I think that fracturing of the MAHA movement is real. It was always an uneasy coalition. The thing that’s happened in recent months is a lot of the people who were Kennedy’s strongest supporters have been unhappy with the progress that he’s made, including, in fact, some of his anti-vaccine supporters, who wanted him to take action to pull COVID vaccines from the market. That was the thing they really wanted. That hasn’t happened, so a lot of those people are disappointed. So yeah, I mean, I think it has fractured. But I think it was just always this sort of bizarre coalition.

Harris: Yeah, it’s just that now the fault lines are more recognizable.

Bartlett: That’s right.

Harris: You had a story over the weekend about Secretary Kennedy urging the White House for a new definition of ultra-processed foods, but there’s been some pushback from the White House. Why is that new definition important?

Bartlett: Yeah, it’s a story that Michael Scherer and I have been working on. For months, Kennedy has promised a federal definition of ultra-processed foods. That matters because once you have a definition, you could potentially move forward on putting labels on foods that were ultra-processed, but you have to have that definition first.

He’s been promising that for months. It appears to have been delayed for quite some time, and now the word is that it may be forthcoming, and it may happen. That would certainly be maybe the biggest accomplishment for MAHA because it would potentially set the table for different kinds of dietary guidelines, warnings. And that’s a move that a lot of nutritionists that I talk to are excited about. They think it’s a good first step toward warning people about ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to obesity and diabetes and cancer and a range of other chronic diseases. So that would be a big deal for Kennedy.

Harris: And what has the pushback been?

Bartlett: Kennedy has wanted this definition for ultra-processed foods. He’s wanted this for months. He said much earlier this year on Joe Rogan that the definition would be coming out very soon. And there’s been, apparently sort of behind the scenes, there have been delays in the administration about when exactly this definition could come out, and I think that’s been a source of frustration.

One of Kennedy’s sort of top allies, Calley Means, quit, in part he says, because this definition had been, in his view, slow-rolled. And so, that behind-the-scenes wrangling has been, I think, a frustration to Kennedy and a frustration to some MAHA supporters.

Harris: Just thinking about the next couple of years, we know that Democrats will have control of Congress come January. Is there any indication that Secretary Kennedy is among those who they’re looking to investigate or potentially impeach?

Bartlett: Yeah, that’s a good question. I think it’s gonna be really interesting to see what Democrats do. Annie Andrews, who’s the senator-elect from South Carolina, who’s a pediatrician, really said she was inspired in large part to run because of Kennedy and has talked about holding him accountable. And so, whether that’s something that Congress does I think is gonna be interesting to see. Certainly the possibility of impeachment seems unlikely. But maybe, who knows?

Harris: Secretary Kennedy celebrated Stephen Miller’s recent ascent to chief of staff at the White House following the midterms. What is the nature of that relationship? And does it sort of solidify these ties between MAGA and MAHA?

Bartlett: I think MAHA supporters had been buoyed by Stephen Miller becoming chief of staff. There was at least a perception that his predecessor, Susie Wiles, was holding back some of the priorities of MAHA. And there’s the feeling—Kennedy has said this, and others have suggested this—that Miller is going to be a closer ally, specifically potentially on vaccines. Miller has echoed some of the things Kennedy has said and some of the things that Trump said about pumping shots into babies and we don’t know the long-term effects and this is a medical travesty. It’s worth saying that we actually have studied the long-term effects of these vaccines and that’s, I think, false. But it makes him seem like a kindred spirit to Kennedy, and so that’s gonna be really interesting. Whether Kennedy is in fact more empowered in this regime than he was in the prior one is TBD.

Harris: Even after this Trump administration, there are still vaccine skeptics in the nation. And herd immunity is a large part of why you need folks to get vaccinated. I guess what are you hearing about what it actually will take to rebuild that trust, even beyond this Trump administration?

Bartlett: One of the consequences of having Kennedy as health secretary is a lot of his ideas and frankly his misinformation has this megaphone, and has gotten to people that might not have been aware of it before.

I think we don’t know what the effect of that will be. I think it’s something that, probably, public-health officials are gonna be attempting to clean up for a long time. And we don’t know whether, they’ll say, the loss of elimination status or the concern around measles—is that going to spur more parents to go get their children vaccinated? In some of these hard-hit communities, that has in fact been the effect, which is encouraging. But I think we just don’t know how long it’s gonna take to rebuild that trust, and some of it’s going to start with having a public-health leader who offers sort of clear messaging that’s in line with what we know from the science.

Harris: Well, Tom, thank you so much for your time and for helping us understand all of this better.

Bartlett: Thanks, Adam.

[Music]

Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pisoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday.

You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you wanna support this work and the work of my colleagues here at The Atlantic, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

This article original identified Senator Sheldon Whitehouse as the senator of Idaho, he is in fact the senator of Rhode Island.

title: The Scandinavian Compromise
summary: We live in a divided nation, and for at least the next two years, we’re going to have a divided government, with one party in control of Congress and the other in control of the White House. But never fear: I am here to bring us together. I think I’ve found a model that I believe will give people on...
content:
We live in a divided nation, and for at least the next two years, we’re going to have a divided government, with one party in control of Congress and the other in control of the White House. But never fear: I am here to bring us together. I think I’ve found a model that I believe will give people on the right and the left what they want. And, unusually for a former Wall Street Journal editorial page writer, I’m looking to Scandinavia for inspiration.

As Brink Lindsey argues in his book The Permanent Problem, the two big challenges we face are inclusion and dynamism.

First, inclusion. It’s possible to get distracted by the current arguments about the exact nature of America’s class divide. Progressives emphasize how much wealth is going to the top one percent. People like me emphasize that the top 20 percent has created a caste system separating the highly educated, who rig everything to their benefit, from everybody else, who are left with the scraps. The truth is that both kinds of inequality are terrible. Great nations decline when they become grossly unequal, and America is staring that possibility straight in the face.

Second, dynamism. Yes, it’s true that over the course of this century the American economy has enormously outperformed the economies of Germany, France, Britain, and Japan. But you get no prizes for besting those geezers. The fact is that for the past 50 years, America’s economic growth and productivity numbers have been sluggish and disappointing. This loss of economic dynamism has retarded wage growth, led to fiscal crises, and contributed to a decline in social mobility. In her forthcoming book, Reviving the American Dream, the Brookings Institution economist Isabel Sawhill notes that if America had sustained the productivity growth levels we enjoyed from 1948 to 1973, and if wages had kept pace with productivity, then the average annual earnings for a 25-to-54-year-old worker would be close to $180,000 a year. Instead, we’re living in a country in which the average wage is less than $70,000 a year.

The psychological effect of these two crises is devastating—loss of trust, pessimism, alienation, class resentment, and pervasive economic insecurity.

Historically, responsibility for these two problems has been divided between the major parties. Republicans were the party of dynamism, emphasizing tax cuts, competition, and deregulation. Democrats were the party of inclusion, emphasizing redistribution, public subsidies, and social insurance. Republicans argued that big welfare states lead to stagnation and torpor. Democrats countered that unfettered capitalism leads to concentration of wealth and exploitation. Then along came Donald Trump, who disagreed with both of those frameworks. He offered a worldview based on protection, claiming that tariffs and immigration barriers would produce a revival of manufacturing. But Trump’s economic formula has manifestly failed—there are scarcely more manufacturing jobs now than when he first glided down the golden escalator.

[Teresa Ghilarducci: The welfare state: A terrible name for an essential system]

America no longer has a party that offers a full-throated case for economic growth. Instead, the Republican Party resembles an intellectual black hole as it approaches the post-Trump era. The Democratic Party, meanwhile, is being pulled leftward by a bunch of young socialists who champion tried-and-failed policies such as rent control, putting me in mind of that old Richard Weaver maxim: The problem with the younger generation is that they haven’t read the minutes to the last meeting.

Here’s why I think the Scandinavians offer us a road map out of this morass: They’re less likely to have our mental categories in their heads. They don’t assume that inclusion and dynamism are at war with each other. They don’t believe you have to choose between capitalism and welfare. Scandinavians have the kind of big supportive welfare systems that make lefties pant in admiration, but most Scandinavians see no contradiction between these systems and aggressive free-market policies. Every year, the libertarian Cato Institute ranks nations in its Human Freedom Index. The Cato ranking system rewards nations for their rule of law, low regulations, free trade, smallish government, property rights, and freedom of religion and expression. In the Cato freedom index, Denmark, Finland, and Sweden all rank higher than the United States.

Some people think of the Scandinavian nations as progressive nirvanas. The story is more complicated than that. For example, the Swedish economist Andreas Bergh divides his country’s economic history into a series of eras. First came the period of 1870 to 1970, when Sweden rose from abject poverty and became one of the richest nations in Europe. There were a lot of causes for this ascent, but my favorite is the Bildung educational policies that the Swedes adopted in the 19th century. They understood that if their kids were going to contribute to an industrial economy, they would need complex inner lives. They would need to understand complex systems. They would have to take more responsibility for the people and national organizations around them. The Bildung approach to education was a human-capital grand slam.

Sweden’s second economic era, according to Bergh, lasted from 1970 to 1995. The country took its newfound wealth and veered left, increasing the tax burden and the size of government, while gradually transferring corporate ownership to funds connected with organized labor. This is the version of Sweden often valorized on the left, but it’s not the end of the story.

In the 1990s, Swedes across the political spectrum realized: Holy Crap! Our economy is tanking, and we won’t have the tax revenues to fund our welfare state! That led to a series of free-market reforms—cutting marginal tax rates, reducing taxes on capital, and increasing competition in a series of formerly regulated sectors, including telecom, electricity, aviation, postal services, and financial markets. Bergh emphasizes that these reforms were not adopted in a ruthlessly partisan manner. Social Democrats acknowledged the need for a dynamic capitalist economy, while conservatives accepted the welfare state. The country rebuilt a competitive market economy while shoring up its social-insurance system.

Today, if you look across Northern Europe, you will see a bunch of policies the Democratic Socialists of America would hate: countries with no wealth tax or minimum wage, that embrace school vouchers or low corporate taxes. The Fraser Institute ranks the progressivity of the tax systems in each of the OECD nations. The United States has the most-progressive tax system in the developed world. The Scandinavian nations are clustered around the bottom.

[Derek Thompson: A simple plan to solve all of America’s problems]

If you scan the region, you see a smorgasbord of arrangements that combine dynamism and inclusion. In Denmark, firing people is relatively easy, giving the labor market much-needed flexibility, but unemployed workers receive both substantial income protection and assistance with retraining and job placement. In Sweden, the government generously funds education, but parents have the freedom to choose which school their kids go to, and schools, including for-profit ones, compete for students. Sweden also reduced corporate-tax rates while widening the tax burden through consumption taxes. The Nordic nations pursue full employment—they want people behaving like good capitalists and workers—but they advance that cause with ideas that sound lefty in the American context, such as universal child care and parental leave. These nations have both flexible labor markets and strong unions.

I don’t think that it would work to copy and paste Scandinavian arrangements directly onto American soil. These are (or, at least, used to be) cohesive, high-trust, communal societies with cultures very different from our own. Their institutions work pretty well, while our state capacity is in sharp decline. Their middle classes are willing to pay higher taxes in exchange for public support, but it’s not clear the American middle classes are willing to do that. Denmark has one of the most restrictive immigration policies in Western Europe, which would not be appropriate for a nation of immigrants such as the United States.

Plus, in the past several years, many Scandinavian nations have turned the dial too far over to the inclusion side, at the cost of economic dynamism. Growth and productivity rates have begun falling alarmingly.

Nonetheless, those tall peoples from up north offer a general approach that is worth learning from. They teach us that it is possible to build a productive workforce within a generous welfare state; to provide economic security for individuals while nurturing capitalist creative destruction; to secure people from some of the disruptions of economic modernization, while still encouraging that modernization.

Furthermore, they teach us that there is a difference between protecting people and protecting jobs. You can give somebody economic security without locking them into one specific employer. There is likewise a difference between who pays for a service and who performs it. You can have governments generously pay for services and allow private firms to compete to offer them. The Scandinavians also show the limits of our conception of freedom. In America, we tend to understand freedom as freedom from the state, but how free are you really, if you are free from Uncle Sam but you live under the thumb of that manager you detest at Sam’s Club and you can’t afford to switch jobs?

So this is the trade-off that I’m proposing: Progressives, you’re going to have to live with a world that is friendlier to corporations and billionaires than you might like, but you get those welfare policies you’ve been talking about for decades. Conservatives, you’re going to have to live with a bigger government than you might like, but you get flexible labor markets, free trade, low taxes on investment, and productive workers.

This model has been sitting there for decades. At periodic intervals, a writer pops up to argue that we should adopt it. But political partisans have refused to embrace it because they have succumbed to the idiot’s primary delusion: Someday, the other half of the country is going to be totally defeated, and my side is going to get everything we want. Meanwhile, the intellectuals have been immobilized by their resentments. The lefties are immobilized by their resentments toward all those vulgar B-school types who looked down on them in college. The righties are immobilized by their resentment toward all those “woke” sociology majors who think that they can salvage their disappointing lives by seizing political power.

[Mike Solana: The abundance delusion]

But I stumble toward the end of the Trump era, having reached a few conclusions. American capitalism is not working for many middle-class American families. At the same time, the sort of policies that American progressives support have sent European countries such as France, Italy, and even Germany into what looks like long-term stagnation and decline. We need a new approach that goes hard on both ends: hard on free-market dynamism and hard on economic security. It’s like going to a Chinese restaurant in which you pick a lot of dishes from column A and also a lot from column B and you fit them together on the same plate—it makes for a more satisfying meal.

If I were ordering off the menu, on the inclusion side, I’d support child tax credits and wage subsidies such as the earned-income tax credit. I’d accede to the child-care and family-leave policies that my lefty friends think are important. I’d support stronger unions to defend worker interests. On the dynamism side, I’d support every human-capital policy you can lay your hands on—school reforms such as the kind that have powered the test-score surge in many Republican states; charter schools; better worker training across their lifespan. I’d support ways to increase public support for scientific research significantly. Over time, I’ve become less impressed by the power of tax cuts to spur economic dynamism, but I’ve become more impressed with the power of deregulation. The abundance movement offers many ways to deregulate home construction (though its adherents don’t like it when you use the word “deregulate”). In their book, The Captured Economy, Brink Lindsey and Steven Teles of the Niskanen Center show just how rife our economy is with “regulatory capture”—the many ways that private companies co-opt state power in order to reduce competition. As they write, “State action, by suppressing and misdirecting entrepreneurship and competition, has rendered our economy less innovative and dynamic as well as less fair.”

To pay for all of this, I’d support a tax on consumption rather than a tax on savings and investment. As some economists have long joked, Democrats will come to love consumption taxes when they realize how much revenue they raise, and Republicans will love them when they realize how regressive they are. (It’s also possible to design them so they are not regressive.)

For decades, progressives have talked a lot about equality and conservatives have talked a lot about freedom, but these days, I’d put the emphasis on agency. How can we create a society in which people have more control over their lives, more opportunity to venture forth and build things for themselves? Nobody has any clue what AI is going to do to our economy over the next few decades, so I’d be in favor of empowering people to come up with their own adaptations, their own new forms of labor, and their own new forms of economic organization. I want an economic system that infuses people with a spirit of daring, exploration, curiosity, ambition, and aspiration. For that, you need both a secure base and an open field to explore.

In his book Mass Flourishing, the Nobel laureate Edmund Phelps writes that “the good life requires the intellectual growth that comes from actively engaging the world and the moral growth that comes from creating and exploring in the face of great uncertainty.” Today, like Phelps, I sense that Americans are suffering from an uncharacteristic loss of national nerve. The spirit of venturesomeness is being replaced by a spirit of fear and loss aversion. I want an economy that will encourage people to venture out into the new, to lead brave and satisfying lives. And to get that economy, I’m willing to live with compromises that I wouldn’t have considered a decade ago.

title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
summary: Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charredA crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.The blaze on the ring road, a key a...
content:
Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred

A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

content:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

content:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.
